study.title: Romans 16 - Greetings, discernment and final doxology
study.overview: Romans 16 closes the letter with a network of personal greetings, a warning against people who promote divisions and a doxology that summarizes the heart of the message: God is the only wise man, firm his people for the gospel and receives glory through Jesus Christ. The chapter shows that the Christian faith is not only abstract doctrine; it creates concrete bonds of service, hospitality, cooperation, vigilance and worship. Paul honors men and women who worked, served, hosted, maintained and protected the work of Christ, while calling the church to prudence before false teachers.

outline.title: Recommendation of Febe and greetings to Priscilla and Aquila
outline.explanation: Paul recommends Febe, presented as a servant of the church in Cencreia, and asks the Romans to receive and help her. Then greet Priscilla and Aquila, praises their cooperation and mentions the church that meets in their home, highlighting service, welcoming and missionary partnership.

outline.title: Greetings to many brothers and calling to holy communion
outline.explanation: Paul sends greetings to various Christians known by the name, men and women, some remembered for intense work, fidelity, kinship, hospitality or spiritual maturity. The set shows a diverse church, linked by affection and cooperation. Verse 16 exhorts to the holy kiss and reminds that the churches of Christ also salute them.

outline.title: Warning against dividers and promise of victory over Satan
outline.explanation: After greetings, Paul warns against people who provoke divisions and stumbling contrary to the doctrine received. He guides the church to avoid them, because such people do not serve Christ, but to themselves. At the same time, it encourages believers to be wise in good and innocent as to evil, with the promise that the God of peace will crush Satan under his feet.

outline.title: Final greetings and glorification to the wise God
outline.explanation: Timothy and other co-workers send greetings, along with Tance, the scribe of the letter, Gaius, Erastus, and Fourth. The closure rises to a theological confession: God is powerful to establish believers according to the gospel, according to the revelation of the mystery previously hidden and now manifested in the Scriptures, to lead all nations to the obedience of faith. The letter ends with a doxology to the only wise God through Jesus Christ.

study.context: The notes indicate that Paul had not yet been in Rome when he wrote the letter, which helps explain why he mentions so many people by name without having visited the church. The commentators suggest that he met several of these brothers along travel and missionary displacements. The chapter also preserves the impression of a letter written in the context of an intense network of Christian cooperation, with greetings from collaborators who were with Paul.
study.theology: Romans 16 unites community life and doctrinal truth. First, the church is seen as a body of real people, known by name, of different conditions, with women exercising important roles of service, support and work in the Lord. Febe is presented as someone who served and helped many, including Paul himself, which highlights the dignity of Christian service and hospitality. Priscilla and Aquila show that cooperation in the gospel may involve personal risk and domestic leadership in church life. Then Paul shows that Christian love does not dispense with discernment: unity needs to be protected against teachings and practices that divide and deviate from the doctrine received. Finally, the chapter ends in worship: God is the one who strengthens the people, reveals the mystery of the gospel, calls the nations to the obedience of faith, and receives glory through Jesus Christ. Thus, Christian life appears as a continual response to grace, marked by service, vigilance and praise.

scholarViews.insight: Febe is presented as a church servant in Cencreia, and the text describes it as someone of resources and influence that helped many, including Paul.
Paul closes the letter with great affection; his greetings sanctify common greetings and show that courtesy and Christianity combine well.
Paul recommends Febe as a servant, a deconisa of the church in Cencreia, and the note describes it as a help for many, possibly hospitable with missionaries.

questions: What kind of discreet but decisive service does the church tend to value little, although God uses it to support his work?
How can we practice hospitality and fellowship without losing discernment in the face of teachings that divide and disfigure the gospel?
How can our church unite relational warmth, doctrinal fidelity, and worship of God at the close of his community life?
study.practice: This week, choose a church person who serves behind the scenes and thank him in a concrete way. Also examine a teaching, counsel, or tendency that is generating division: compare it with the doctrine received in the Scriptures and move away from what runs counter to the gospel. Finally, turn your final prayer of the day into doxology, thanking the only wise God for establishing you in Christ.
study.uncertainty: The chapter does not explicitly inform all the biographical details of the cited characters; some identities and family relationships remain uncertain. The notes also suggest, but do not definitively demonstrate, as Paul knew so many Christians in Rome. It is not safe to state beyond what the text and notes allow on positions, social status or the exact composition of these houses and churches.
